```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
strava_runs <- read_csv("data/strava_runs.csv")
```

```{r}
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      distance..m. > 4998 & distance..m. < 5015  ~ "5k",
      distance..m. > 9998 & distance..m. < 10015 ~ "10k",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event))
```


## Exercise 1

When you fill the missing part, remove the # symbol before running the code chunk and eval=FALSE

```{r ex1a, out.width="80%", eval=FALSE}
data_5k_10k %>% 
   filter(gender == "M") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
   ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "M") %>%
  summarise(
    mean_hr = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm= TRUE),
    median_hr = median(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hr = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```


The histogram shows the distribution of average heart rates among male runners. The distribution is not perfectly symmetric. The most observations concentrated between 135-165 bpm. The highest frequency occurs around 145-150 bpm.
The mean average heart rate is 147.94 bpm. The median is 147.9 bpm. Since the mean and median are very similar, the distribution appears to be approximately symmetric around its centre, which is consistent with the histogram. The standard deviation is 17.22 bpm. 

```{r ex1b, out.width="80%"}
data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "F") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.))%>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)
  




```

The histogram for female runners is bimodal, with peaks around 150 bpm and 165-170 bpm. Most observations lie between approximately 140 and 175 bpm.
In comparison, the male heart rate distribution appears more unimodal, with its peak is around 145-150 bpm. Both distributions show variation and overlap in their heart rate ranges. But the female distribution appears less smooth and one more peak.


## Exercise 2

```{r ex2, out.width = "80%"}
data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender))%>%
  mutate(
    pace = (elapsed.time..s./60)/
      (distance..m. /1000),
    event = factor(event, level = c("5k","10k"))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = event, y = pace))+
  geom_boxplot() + 
  facet_wrap(~ gender) +
  labs(
    title = "Running Pace by Distance and Gender",
    x = "Running distance",
    y = "Pace (min/km)"
  )




```

The boxplots compare running pace for 5K and 10K runs by gender. Among female runners, the median pace is similar for the two distances, at around 6 minutes per kilometer. Among male runners, the median pace is lower for 10K than for 5K, suggesting faster running over 10K in the dataset. Both genders show some high-pace outliers, and the 5K runs for male runners appear to have greater variability. In conclusion, the male runners have lower median pace values than female runners in the dataset.




## Exercise 3

```{r ex3, out.width = "80%"}
athlete_distance <- strava_runs %>%
  filter(!is.na(distance..m.)) %>%
  group_by(athlete)%>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance = mean(distance..m.)/1000
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    runner_type = case_when(
      mean_distance > 13 ~ "Long-distance",
      mean_distance < 7 ~ "Short-distance",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

data_speed <- strava_runs%>%
  left_join(
    athlete_distance %>%
      select(athlete,runner_type),
    by = "athlete"
  )%>%
  filter(!is.na(runner_type))%>%
  filter(
    !is.na(distance..m.),
    !is.na(elapsed.time..s.),
    elapsed.time..s.>0
  )%>%
  mutate(
    distance_km = distance..m./1000,
    speed = distance..m./elapsed.time..s.
  )
data_speed %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = distance_km,
    y = speed,
    colour= runner_type
  ))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",se= FALSE)+
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Long-distance" = "orange",
      "Short-distance"= "forestgreen"
    )
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Running Distance and Average Speed",
    x = "Distance (km)",
    y = "Average speed (m/s)",
    color = "Runner type"
  )
  




```

The scatter plot shows the relationship between running distance and average speed for short-distance and long-distance runners. The trend lines suggest a negative relationship between distance speed in both groups, particularly for short-distance runners. The negative trend is weaker for long-distance runners. However, the points are widely scattered and the two groups overlap considerably, indicating substantial variation in speed at similar distances. These results show an association rather than a causal relationship.


## Exercise 4

```{r ex4, out.width = "80%"}
strava_runs%>%
  group_by(gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance = mean(distance..m.,na.rm = TRUE)/1000,
    mean_time = mean (elapsed.time..s.,na.rm = TRUE)/60
  )%>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_distance, mean_time),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "average"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      mean_distance = "Average distance (km)",
      mean_time = "Average elapsed time (min)"
    )
  )%>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = average))+
  geom_col()+
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales= "free_y")+
  labs(
    title = "Average Running Distance and Time by Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Average value"
  )





```


The bar charts compare the mean running distance and mean elapsed time by gender. Male runners have a higher mean running distance than demale runners in this dataset. However, the mean elapsed times for male and female runners are very similar, with females having a silghtly higher mean. These are decriptive comparsions of the recorded runs and do not establish that gendeer causes the difference.
